title: What Is Critical Thinking — and Why Does It Matter?
description: Explicit introduction to Critical Thinking as Unit 1's durable skill. Critical thinking is the ability to analyze and evaluate information in order to make objective, well-reasoned decisions — rather than reacting based on assumptions, first impressions, or what others tell you to think. In a career exploration unit, critical thinking is essential: every career research decision, every evaluation of salary data or job outlook, every comparison across the Career Exploration Matrix is an act of critical thinking. Students explore: What is the difference between having an opinion and having a reasoned position? How do you know when a source is reliable? What does it look like to evaluate a career claim vs. accept it?

title: What Is Growth Mindset — and Why Does It Matter?
description: Explicit introduction to Growth Mindset as Unit 3's durable skill. Growth mindset is the belief that abilities, intelligence, and character can be developed through effort, strategy, and learning from setbacks — as opposed to a fixed mindset that treats these as static. In a pathways unit, growth mindset is critical: choosing a postsecondary path involves uncertainty, and students who believe they can grow into the challenges ahead are far more likely to persist and succeed. Students explore: What is the difference between a growth mindset and toxic positivity? What does growth mindset look like when a pathway gets hard? How does it connect to the resilience they have already shown in their own life maps?

unit_name: Unit 2: How Can My Career Make a Difference in the World?  |  Durable Skill Introduced: Creativity  |  Milestone(s): Modified Impact Proposal
title: What Is Creativity — and Why Does It Matter?
description: Explicit introduction to Creativity as Unit 2's durable skill. Creativity is the ability to generate original ideas, make unexpected connections, and approach problems in novel ways — it is not just about art, but about how you think. In a unit about Global Pressing Challenges, creativity is the engine: the world's hardest problems have not been solved yet because they require new thinking. Students who can see possibilities others miss, combine ideas from different fields, and propose solutions that do not yet exist are exactly who the world needs. Students explore: What does creativity actually look like in a professional context? Can you be creative in finance, medicine, engineering, or policy? What conditions help you think most originally?

title: What Are All the Ways I Can Reach My Career Goals?
description: All roads lead somewhere — multiple ways to get to careers. 4-Year College and Community College: structure, costs, timeline, completion rates, ROI. Understanding debt and financial planning.

unit_name: Unit 3: How Do I Get from Here to There?  |  Durable Skill Introduced: Growth Mindset  |  Milestone(s): Pathways Analysis Document + Pathways Presentation
title: What Is Growth Mindset — and Why Does It Matter?
description: Explicit introduction to Growth Mindset as Unit 3's durable skill. Growth mindset is the belief that abilities, intelligence, and character can be developed through effort, strategy, and learning from setbacks — as opposed to a fixed mindset that treats these as static. In a pathways unit, growth mindset is critical: choosing a postsecondary path involves uncertainty, and students who believe they can grow into the challenges ahead are far more likely to persist and succeed. Students explore: What is the difference between a growth mindset and toxic positivity? What does growth mindset look like when a pathway gets hard? How does it connect to the resilience they have already shown in their own life maps?
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'Think of a time you got better at something you once thought you were bad at. What made the difference — and what does that tell you about what you are capable of?'

unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume
title: What Does It Mean to Lead Yourself?
description: Explicit Leadership introduction. What is leadership as a durable skill — and why does it start with self-leadership before it extends to others? Reframes resume and portfolio work as acts of leadership: taking ownership, making strategic decisions, advocating for yourself. Students begin to see themselves as the executive of their own future.

unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume
title: What Does Thriving Actually Look Like?
description: Introduction to the idea that what you do matters as much as where you go. Research shows that certain types of experiences — mentorship, applied learning, community engagement, skill development — predict success across all postsecondary pathways. Students begin thinking about what they've already built and what they still want to build before graduation. Sets up the portfolio audit with genuine purpose.

unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume
title: Who Have I Become? — Strengths & Interests Update
description: Structured portfolio audit focused on Strengths and Interests. Students return to their 9th grade 'Who I Am' statement, Values Statements, and 10th grade Career Vision — what has shifted, deepened, or clarified since then? Update platform portfolio with current Strengths (min. 5) and Interests (min. 5).

unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume
title: What Have I Done? — Experience Inventory
description: Comprehensive audit of all experiences: work, volunteer, extracurricular, academic projects, leadership roles, community involvement. Structured inventory protocol to capture everything — including experiences students might undervalue or overlook. Emphasis on depth over polish at this stage: get it all on paper first. Begins updating Work Experience section of platform portfolio.

unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume
title: Where Do I Stand?
description: An honest inventory of who you are right now as a junior. What experiences have shaped you? What skills have you actually developed? What roles have you played — in school, at home, in your community — that say something real about who you're becoming? Structured self-assessment protocol requiring evidence. Less about checking boxes, more about seeing yourself clearly. Normalizes gaps as actionable information, not failure.

unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume
title: What's Still Possible?
description: Junior year is not the end of the story. What experiences do you still want to have before graduation? What kind of person do you want to be by the time you walk across that stage? Students set 1-2 concrete intentions — not rigid goals, but genuine directions. Completes portfolio update — all sections finalized and uploaded. Students enter goal(s) into Willow platform.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (7 min): 'What do you still want to build or experience before graduation? What kind of person do you want to be by the time you finish high school?'

unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume
title: What Makes a Resume Work? + How Does It Come Together?
description: Combined lesson: analyzing strong resume examples across multiple contexts — scholarship applications, employment, postsecondary program applications — to develop shared evaluative criteria (what makes a resume compelling? what makes one fall flat?), then resume fundamentals: standard sections, formatting principles, language conventions, action verbs. unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume
title: From Portfolio to Resume
description: The translation lesson — explicitly connecting portfolio content to resume language with examples. Key insight: the portfolio is the raw material, the resume is the curated presentation. Nothing is invented here — everything comes from work students have already done. Students practice translating 2-3 of their own portfolio entries into resume language.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What feels most important to communicate about yourself through your resume? What do you want someone to know about you before they've even met you?'

unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume
title: Drafting — All Sections
description: Single comprehensive drafting session covering all sections: Education, Experience, Activities, Skills, and any additional sections relevant to individual students. Students make decisions about what to include and what to omit — a leadership moment. Teacher circulates for support. Every student leaves with a complete rough draft.

unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume
title: Language + Tailoring
description: Combined lesson: upgrading language with action verbs and specificity (before/after examples; the difference between 'helped with events' and 'coordinated logistics for 3 annual fundraising events serving 200+ community members') + principles of strategic tailoring for different audiences — scholarship applications, employment, postsecondary programs. Students revise their full draft applying both principles.

unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume
title: Peer Feedback + Revision
description: Structured peer feedback protocol on complete resume drafts — feedback focused on completeness, language strength, clarity, and whether the resume accurately represents who this person is. Students give and receive feedback, then begin substantive revision based on peer input.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What was the most useful piece of feedback you received? What did it help you see about how others perceive you?'

unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume
title: Self-Review + Alma Review
description: Detailed checklist-based self-review: does every bullet start with an action verb? Is every experience dated? Are there quantifiable details? Are all sections complete? Then Alma-assisted review with targeted questions about resume content. Three feedback lenses complete: peer, self-review, and Alma. Students make final targeted revisions.

unit_name: Unit 1: Show the World Who You Are  |  Durable Skill: Leadership  |  Milestones: Updated Portfolio + Polished Resume

Reframes list-building and matrix work as communication challenges: how do you articulate your thinking clearly, defend your reasoning with evidence, and present your decisions compellingly to others?

unit_name: Unit 2: Find Where You Belong  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestones: Balanced List (8 programs) + Program Comparison Matrix with Rationale
title: Who Am I Bringing Into This Search?
description: Content lesson where students actively build their personal fit criteria by synthesizing their 9th and 10th grade portfolio work — Mission Statement, Career Vision, Values Statements. alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What do you already know about yourself that should shape where you look? What would it feel like to be in the right place?'

description: Structured review of all six pathway types from 10th grade. Explicit framing: you know what these pathways are — now we're going to evaluate specific programs within them. unit_name: Unit 2: Find Where You Belong  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestones: Balanced List (8 programs) + Program Comparison Matrix with Rationale
title: From Pathway to Program — How Do I Evaluate What's Inside?
description: The critical shift from pathway awareness to program evaluation. What questions should you be asking about any specific program, regardless of pathway type? Introduction to evaluation criteria: selectivity, completion rates, program-specific outcomes, cost, and what students like you actually experience there. Key insight: two programs in the same pathway can look completely different when you look closely.

unit_name: Unit 2: Find Where You Belong  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestones: Balanced List (8 programs) + Program Comparison Matrix with Rationale
title: What Is ROI and Why Does It Matter?
description: Conceptual introduction to Return on Investment as an educational decision-making framework. Real, concrete, sometimes surprising examples across pathway types. Central insight: what you study is often as important as where you study. Discussion-driven — no platform yet. Students examine examples challenging assumptions about which credentials are 'worth it.'

unit_name: Unit 2: Find Where You Belong  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestones: Balanced List (8 programs) + Program Comparison Matrix with Rationale
title: Reading ROI on the Willow Platform

Teacher-facilitated walkthrough of institutional ROI, program-specific ROI, and personalized ROI (accounts for income bracket and Pell likelihood). Students practice navigating to ROI data for programs they're already curious about.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What surprised you about the ROI data you found? Did any program look different than you expected once you saw the numbers?'

unit_name: Unit 2: Find Where You Belong  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestones: Balanced List (8 programs) + Program Comparison Matrix with Rationale
title: Completion Rates — Will Students Like Me Actually Finish?

Students find and interpret completion rate data by race/ethnicity, first-gen status, and Pell grant recipient status on the platform. Key reframe: a school with a 90% overall graduation rate and a 55% first-gen graduation rate is telling you something important.

unit_name: Unit 2: Find Where You Belong  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestones: Balanced List (8 programs) + Program Comparison Matrix with Rationale

How do personal fit criteria interact with quality data?
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'Based on what you've learned about quality, what matters most to YOU in evaluating a program? How has your thinking shifted since the start of this unit?'

unit_name: Unit 2: Find Where You Belong  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestones: Balanced List (8 programs) + Program Comparison Matrix with Rationale

Students leave with a clear search strategy and initial program pool.

Structured research protocol: for each program, what do I know about fit, quality indicators, and how it connects to my Career Vision? unit_name: Unit 2: Find Where You Belong  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestones: Balanced List (8 programs) + Program Comparison Matrix with Rationale

unit_name: Unit 2: Find Where You Belong  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestones: Balanced List (8 programs) + Program Comparison Matrix with Rationale

unit_name: Unit 2: Find Where You Belong  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestones: Balanced List (8 programs) + Program Comparison Matrix with Rationale

Structured narrowing protocol: which programs genuinely excite you, align with your Career Vision, meet quality thresholds, and feel like realistic fits? Students make difficult decisions about what to cut and articulate why — Communication in action.

unit_name: Unit 2: Find Where You Belong  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestones: Balanced List (8 programs) + Program Comparison Matrix with Rationale

For students pursuing other pathways: equivalent categorization logic. Students begin categorizing their preliminary list. Key message: a balanced list is a strategic document, not a wish list.

description: Introduction to the Program Comparison Matrix as a communication artifact. What is it, what does it need to contain, and why does the rationale column matter as much as the data columns? description: Students populate data columns of matrix for all eight programs. For each program they begin drafting rationale. Emphasis on specificity: 'program-specific ROI of $340K and 87% first-gen completion rate align with my financial goals and career direction in engineering' is rationale. 'Good ROI' is not.

title: Strengthening the Rationale — Session A
description: Deep focus on rationale quality. Students audit their rationale against Communication criteria: Is it specific? Is it evidence-based? Does it connect to personal fit criteria and Career Vision? Does it distinguish this program from others? Students revise and strengthen rationale with peer support.

unit_name: Unit 2: Find Where You Belong  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestones: Balanced List (8 programs) + Program Comparison Matrix with Rationale

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: From List to Story
description: Unit launch bridging from Unit 2. Students have found where they belong — now they need to tell those programs who they are in their own voice. What is a personal statement and why does it matter? Key reframe: admissions readers want a real person, not a perfect student. Students read 1–2 short personal statement excerpts cold and discuss: what do you notice? Introduction to unit arc: generate → analyze → select → draft → revise → polish.

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: What Is Fortitude and Why Does It Matter Now?
description: Explicit Fortitude introduction. What is fortitude as a durable skill — resilience, persistence, optimism in the face of difficulty? Why is it introduced here? The personal statement requires vulnerability, tolerance for imperfection, and persistence through revision. Brief writing exercise: describe a time you stuck with something difficult. Pair share. Not essay material — a warm-up connecting the durable skill to lived experience.

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: What Story Do I Have to Tell? — Mining the Portfolio
description: Before any writing begins, students systematically review their 9th–11th grade portfolio work — Mission Statement, Values Statements, "Who I Am" statement, Career Vision, Impact Project, and resume. What themes keep emerging? What moments feel unfinished or unexplored? This is not writing yet — it's inventory and noticing. Output: a personal story inventory of 8–10 potential story directions.

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: What Makes a Personal Statement Work?
description: Analysis of 3–4 strong personal statement examples across different voices, stories, and backgrounds — deliberately chosen to represent diversity of topic, tone, and structure. Teacher-facilitated close reading: what is each writer doing? What makes each essay feel authentic rather than generic? Students develop shared evaluative criteria: specificity, voice, structure, authenticity, insight. Materials must include annotated anchor examples — criteria are built from concrete textual evidence, not abstract discussion. These criteria become the backbone of every feedback conversation later in the unit.

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Deconstructing the Craft
description: Deeper analysis of craft decisions in strong personal statements. How does a writer find and develop a story? How do you open without a cliché? How do you move between narrative and reflection? How do you end with insight rather than summary? Key insight: voice means writing the way you actually think, not the way you think you're supposed to sound. Students identify 2–3 craft moves they want to try.
platform_action: Annotated examples with craft moves noted

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Generative Writing — Getting It Out
description: Low-stakes, time-pressured writing exercises designed to generate raw material in authentic voice — before any pressure of "this is my essay." Three or four timed prompts (8–10 min each): a moment you'll never forget, a place that shaped you, a time something didn't go as planned, something you know how to do that most people don't. No editing, no stopping. Teacher models first.

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Selecting Your Story
description: Students make the pivotal decision: which story to develop into their personal statement. Structured selection protocol: review story inventory and raw writing — where is the most authentic energy? Which story is only yours to tell? Which has room for genuine reflection? Peer conversation: partners share top two story candidates and discuss which feels more compelling. Students commit to one story direction with brief written rationale.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): "Why is this the story you need to tell? What do you want someone to know about you after reading it?"

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Voice: Writing the Way You Actually Think
description: Concrete, scaffolded instruction on voice. Show a generic version of a passage side-by-side with the version that sounds like a real person — what changed? Name the moves: sentence length variation, real language vs. "essay voice," specificity of detail. Teacher models revising a generic sentence into authentic voice. Students take 2–3 sentences from their raw writing and revise toward authentic voice using a protocol: read aloud → does this sound like me? → rewrite until it does. Partner share: read both versions aloud, partner identifies which sounds more real.

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Structure: Mapping Your Story
description: How does a personal statement move? Not a five-paragraph essay. Four-box story map: Where does your story start? (drop into a moment) → What happens? (the experience unfolds) → What did you realize? (reflection/insight) → Where does it land? (what this means going forward). Teacher pulls up 1–2 examples from L4–L5 to show structure inside them. Students sketch their own story map. Teacher circulates with specific prompts for stuck students: "Tell me out loud — where does your story actually start?" Students who finish early begin drafting their opening paragraph.

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Drafting Session A
description: First full drafting session. Students write with story map as guide. Structured checkpoint at minute 20: students read their last sentence aloud to a partner; if stuck, tell partner where. Teacher circulates using conferring guide built into materials with prompts for common stuck points (all setup/no scene → "Pick one moment and describe just that"; can't start → "Tell me the story out loud"; writing someone else's voice → "Read this out loud — is that how you'd say it to a friend?"). Every student leaves with a partial draft.

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Drafting Session B
description: Continued drafting. Brief targeted craft tip based on teacher observation from L10 (materials include 3–4 "common issue" mini-lessons teacher can choose from: opening in the middle of a moment, being specific instead of general, reflection that says something real). Structured checkpoint at minute 20. Students who finish early reread for voice. Most students should have a complete or near-complete draft.

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Drafting Session C / Complete Draft
description: Final drafting session. For students with complete drafts: read beginning to end, don't fix anything, just notice and mark strongest/weakest sections. For students still drafting: today is the day you finish. Fallback protocol for students under 400 words: work with teacher or partner to talk through the missing section out loud before writing it. Every student leaves with a complete rough draft of approximately 650 words.

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Revision as a Skill
description: Explicit instruction on revision as a distinct skill. What is the difference between editing (surface corrections) and revision (substantive improvement)? Five revision lenses: opening strength, voice consistency, specificity of detail, quality of reflection, closing resonance. Teacher models a revision read on a sample draft — thinking aloud through each lens, identifying the highest-leverage fix. Students practice applying the five lenses to the same sample draft and identify three highest-leverage revision priorities.
platform_action: Revision framework notes + practice annotations on sample

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Feedback as a Skill
description: Feedback uses the same five lenses as revision — applied to someone else's work. What makes feedback useful vs. vague? ("I liked it" = not useful. "Your opening drops me into the kitchen, but then the second paragraph jumps to a summary — I lost the scene" = useful.) Norms for giving: lead with what's working, be specific, focus on writing not the person. Norms for receiving: listen first, ask clarifying questions, you decide what to use. Teacher models on sample draft. LOW-STAKES REHEARSAL: partners practice giving feedback on the same sample draft (not their own essays).

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Self-Review + First Revision Pass
description: Students apply revision framework to their own draft. Step 1 — Read aloud to self (10 min): read draft aloud quietly, mark places where you stumble, lose track, or hear something off. No analysis yet — just feel it. Step 2 — Checklist self-review (15 min): apply five lenses, annotate draft, identify three highest-leverage revision priorities. Step 3 — Begin revising (15 min): address at least one priority.
platform_action: Annotated draft + revision priorities + first revision pass

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Peer Feedback
description: Structured peer feedback on complete drafts. Revisit feedback norms from L14 — this time it's real, someone's actual story. Acknowledge courage required on both sides (Fortitude connection). Partners read, annotate, and discuss. Feedback focused on: where does voice feel most authentic? Where is the story underdeveloped? Where does reflection feel genuine vs. generic? Where were you most engaged as a reader? Written feedback using structured protocol.

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Revision Session: Using Peer Feedback
description: How to read feedback strategically: you don't have to use everything. Look for patterns — if your partner and your self-review flagged the same thing, that's a priority. Make a revision plan. Full work time for substantive revision implementing peer feedback alongside self-review insights. Teacher circulates with conferring guide.

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Alma-Assisted Review + Revision Planning
description: Alma is the third feedback lens — surfaces things self and peer may have missed. Targeted Alma questions: Does this opening make me want to keep reading? Where does your voice feel most like you? What's the most important insight — is it clear? Students synthesize all three feedback sources (self, peer, Alma) into a final revision plan. Explicit progress framing: compare current draft to rough draft and name what's better. Begin implementing final substantive revisions.
platform_action: Alma review notes + final revision plan + revised draft
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma-assisted review with targeted questions about draft quality, voice, and insight

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Final Substantive Revision
description: Last substantive revision session. Last check: are you revising or just editing? Today is for the last big moves — voice consistency, specificity, and reflection quality. After today, we shift to polish. Full work time with teacher conferring support. Students implement remaining revision plan items. Read essay beginning to end: does it sound like you? Does it say what you mean?

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Final Polish
description: Shift from revision to polish — sentence-level clarity, word choice, flow, transitions, length calibration to 650 words. Read-aloud protocol with partner: hear where it sounds natural and where it stumbles. Final surface editing. Check against evaluative criteria from Phase 2. Final self-assessment: is this application-ready? Does it accurately represent who I am?

unit_name: Unit 3: Tell Your Story In Your Own Voice  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone: Application-Ready Personal Statement (650 words)
title: Upload + Milestone Celebration
description: One final read. Quality check protocol — one last look before uploading. Upload polished personal statement to platform Personal Statement section. Milestone complete. Brief individual reflection: what does it mean to have this done? Whole-class acknowledgment and voluntary sharing.

unit_name: Unit 1: This Is Your Year  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Senior Year Action Plan
title: What Is Collaboration and Why Does It Define Senior Year?
description: Explicit Collaboration introduction as the year's capstone durable skill. Senior year is not a solo project: it requires asking for help, coordinating with family, advocating with counselors and teachers, and eventually building a new community from scratch. Reframes collaboration not as group work but as the skill of building and activating the right support network at the right moment.

unit_name: Unit 1: This Is Your Year  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Senior Year Action Plan

Students return to their full Willow portfolio — Mission Statement, Career Vision, Values Statements, resume, list, matrix — with fresh eyes. What has changed? What feels more true than ever? What needs updating? Students note 2-3 things they want to adjust or deepen. This is calibration, not a rebuild.

unit_name: Unit 1: This Is Your Year  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Senior Year Action Plan
title: Building Your Support System
description: Collaboration made concrete. Who are the five people whose support will matter most this year: a teacher who knows your work, a counselor who knows your goals, a family member who will help with FAFSA, a peer going through this alongside you, and a mentor in a field you care about. Students map their support system and identify any gaps. Introduction to the ask: how do you request support in a way that is specific and gracious?
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'Who has shown up for you in ways that have mattered? Who do you want in your corner this year, and what will you ask of them?'

unit_name: Unit 1: This Is Your Year  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Senior Year Action Plan
title: Understanding the Senior Year Calendar
description: The full arc of the year made visible. Students map all major deadlines onto a personal calendar: EA/ED deadlines (November 1/15), FAFSA opening (October 1), Regular Decision deadlines (typically January 1), scholarship deadlines (rolling, starting fall), financial aid award letters (March–April), National Decision Day (May 1). Key insight: the calendar runs on schools' schedules — which means students must plan backward from deadlines.

unit_name: Unit 1: This Is Your Year  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Senior Year Action Plan
title: The Senior Year Action Plan
description: Students build a personal action plan for the full year: application timeline (which schools, which deadlines, EA/ED or RD?), FAFSA preparation checklist, scholarship targets and deadlines, decision criteria they want to apply in spring. This is a living document — it will evolve — but having a plan changes how the year unfolds.

unit_name: Unit 1: This Is Your Year  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Senior Year Action Plan
title: First-Gen Identity and the College-Going Culture
description: Identity-affirming lesson on what it means to be first-generation in a college-going culture that was not designed for you. Names the hidden curriculum directly: what you don't know because no one in your family has been there yet is a structural issue, not a personal failure. Peer conversation: what do you want college to be for you that it couldn't be for the generation before you?
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What does being first-gen mean to you? What do you want college to be that it couldn't be for the generation before you?'

unit_name: Unit 1: This Is Your Year  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Senior Year Action Plan
title: Asking for What You Need
description: The practical skill of making requests — from teachers for recommendations, from counselors for support, from family members for FAFSA documents, from programs for fee waivers. Students practice the anatomy of a strong ask: specific, time-bounded, context-setting, and gracious. Role-play: practice asking a teacher for a recommendation letter. Students leave with a plan for their first three asks of the year.

unit_name: Unit 1: This Is Your Year  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Senior Year Action Plan
title: End-of-Unit Alma Synthesis + Celebration
description: Full end-of-unit structure: Teacher-facilitated communal reflection (10 min) — naming what students have built over three years and what this year means → Peer conversation (10 min): 'What do you want this year to mean for you?' → Alma synthesis (10-15 min) → Closing celebration (10 min).
alma_integration: Full end-of-unit Alma structure

unit_name: Unit 2: Understanding Financial Aid Before It Opens  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): FAFSA-Ready Checklist + Parent/Guardian Communication Plan
title: Why Financial Aid Starts Now
description: Unit launch. FAFSA opens October 1 — preparation must happen in September. What financial aid actually is: federal grants, institutional grants, loans, and work-study. Key reframe: filing FAFSA is the single highest-ROI action a first-gen family can take. The cost of not filing is enormous.

unit_name: Unit 2: Understanding Financial Aid Before It Opens  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): FAFSA-Ready Checklist + Parent/Guardian Communication Plan
title: The Financial Aid System — How It Actually Works
description: Demystifying the full financial aid system. The Student Aid Index (SAI): what it is and what it means for award amounts. Types of aid: federal Pell Grant, institutional grants, subsidized vs. unsubsidized loans, work-study. Key insight: most families drastically underestimate how much institutional grant aid high-need students receive at certain institutions. Sticker price vs. net price distinction.

unit_name: Unit 2: Understanding Financial Aid Before It Opens  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): FAFSA-Ready Checklist + Parent/Guardian Communication Plan
title: Who Qualifies and What You'll Need
description: Eligibility basics: citizenship, enrollment status, dependency rules. Special circumstances: undocumented students, students in foster care, homeless youth. Documents needed: Social Security numbers, tax returns (prior-prior year), W-2s, bank statements, untaxed income records. Collaboration in action: this requires a family conversation.

unit_name: Unit 2: Understanding Financial Aid Before It Opens  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): FAFSA-Ready Checklist + Parent/Guardian Communication Plan
title: The Family Conversation About FAFSA
description: The hardest part of FAFSA is often not the form itself but the conversation with parents or guardians about income and assets. Students prepare for this conversation: what information they need, how to explain why it matters, what to do if a parent is reluctant or unavailable. Special circumstances addressed: non-filing parents, parents with mixed immigration status, estranged parents.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What feels hardest about having this conversation with your family? What do you most need them to understand?'

unit_name: Unit 2: Understanding Financial Aid Before It Opens  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): FAFSA-Ready Checklist + Parent/Guardian Communication Plan
title: Setting Up and Navigating the FAFSA
description: Hands-on orientation to studentaid.gov. Creating FSA IDs (both student and parent/guardian). Walkthrough of the form structure. Common mistakes to avoid. Schools to list on FAFSA. Priority filing dates: some state and institutional programs have first-come-first-served funding. Students leave with FSA IDs created or a plan to create them.
student_work_product: FSA ID created + FAFSA filing plan

unit_name: Unit 2: Understanding Financial Aid Before It Opens  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): FAFSA-Ready Checklist + Parent/Guardian Communication Plan
title: What Happens After You Submit
description: The timeline after filing: Student Aid Report (SAR) arrives within 3-5 business days, review it for errors, schools receive your information. Verification: some students are selected — this requires additional documentation. Special circumstances appeals: if your family's financial situation has changed, you can request a professional judgment review.

unit_name: Unit 2: Understanding Financial Aid Before It Opens  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): FAFSA-Ready Checklist + Parent/Guardian Communication Plan
title: FAFSA Simulation + Questions
description: Guided simulation using sample student scenarios — realistic examples that walk through the full form. Students practice identifying where each piece of information goes and what to do when something doesn't fit neatly. Q&A: every question is valid. Students finalize their FAFSA-Ready Checklist and set their filing date.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What do you understand about financial aid now that you didn't before? What is the one thing you need to do this week to move toward filing?'

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: What You're Actually Building
description: Unit launch. The application is not a form — it's a curated self-presentation. Everything students have built since 9th grade is raw material. Introduction to Common App as the primary platform for most four-year applications, with explicit acknowledgment that students pursuing other pathways have different processes — this unit differentiates by pathway where needed.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: What Is Fortitude and Why Does It Matter Right Now?
description: Explicit Fortitude return — introduced in 11th grade Unit 3 for the personal statement, now applied at scale. Applications are exhausting. Deadlines create stress. Rejection is coming for almost everyone. Brief reflection: where did you demonstrate fortitude during personal statement writing? What will you draw on now?
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'Where did you show fortitude during your personal statement process last year? What did you do when it got hard? What will you draw on now?'

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: The Application Ecosystem
description: Full orientation to Common App vs. Coalition App vs. school-specific portals. How accounts work, how to add schools, what sections exist. Teacher walkthrough of Common App structure: profile, family, education, testing, activities, writing, courses & grades. Students create Common App accounts; students on other pathways get orientation to their specific portals.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Profile, Family, and Education Sections
description: Working session: students complete Profile, Family, and Education sections. Most of this is factual — the skill is precision and completeness. Common pitfalls: leaving fields blank, entering GPA incorrectly, misunderstanding class rank. Every student leaves with these three sections complete.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Testing and Honors
description: Test-optional landscape: what it means and how to navigate it. When to submit test scores: guidance on whether a score strengthens or weakens an application. Honors section: every award, honor, recognition — academic, community, school-based. Teacher protocol: if it had your name on it, it counts.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: The Activities List — Drafting and Completion
description: The activities section: 10 entries, each with 150 characters for description. Bridging from the 11th grade resume: the resume is the raw material, the activities list is the curated version. Teacher models translation of resume entries into 150-character descriptions using action verbs and specificity. Students draft and complete all entries in a single focused session. Peer check: is this list accurate and complete?
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What do you want someone to see about you through your activities list that they might not expect?'

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Activities List Peer Review + Finalization
description: Structured peer review of complete activities lists. Review criteria: Is every description specific and active? Does the list feel authentic to this person? Are there entries that should be cut or reordered? Are there experiences missing? Students give written feedback, revise, and finalize. Teacher conferences with students who have fewer than 7 substantive entries.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Understanding Recommendations
description: What recommendation letters actually do: they provide a third-party perspective on character, intellectual engagement, growth, and potential. What makes a strong recommender: someone who knows you well, has seen you grow, and can speak with specificity. Two teacher recommendations + counselor recommendation. Students identify their recommenders.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Requesting Recommendations
description: The formal ask — done well. Students draft and deliver recommendation requests: a letter or email that provides context and specifics. The ask is practice in collaboration: you are asking someone to invest significant time on your behalf. Gratitude and specificity go together. Students send requests in this lesson.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Supporting Your Recommenders
description: Students create a recommender support packet: resume, activities list, personal statement draft, a one-pager with 3-4 specific memories from the class. Follow-up timing: a polite check-in two weeks before any deadline. The counselor recommendation — what your counselor needs from you and how to have that conversation.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Returning to Your Story — Fresh Eyes and Final Revision
description: Students retrieve their personal statements from 11th grade Unit 3 and read with fresh eyes: what still feels true? What has changed? What feels underdeveloped with nine more months of perspective? Most students will not rewrite from scratch — they need targeted refinements. Students who genuinely need a deeper pass get a differentiated pathway. Peer read: does this still sound like you? Students make final revisions based on fresh perspective and any peer feedback.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What do you want this essay to say about you that your grades and activities can't? What part of your story feels most true right now?'

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Final Polish + Upload to Common App
description: Students make final polish — sentence-level clarity, word choice, word count check (650 maximum) — then read aloud one final time before uploading to Common App. Quality check: does this represent me accurately and compellingly? Teacher available for any last questions. Personal statement upload complete.
student_work_product: Personal statement uploaded to Common App

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Understanding Supplements + 'Why Us?' Deep Dive
description: What supplemental essays are and why they exist. Inventory of supplement requirements across all schools on the student's list — length, prompts, deadlines. Deep focus on the 'Why Us?' essay: what admissions readers look for (specificity, genuine research, authentic enthusiasm) vs. what makes these essays fall flat (generic programs lists, rankings, anything that could be copy-pasted to another school). Students begin research for top 2-3 schools.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Other Common Supplementals — Know What You're Writing
description: The full range of supplement types beyond 'Why Us?': Why This Major (connects academic interest to lived experience and career direction), Diversity/Community essay (what perspective do you bring that enriches a campus community), Short Answer questions (activities, challenges, intellectual interests — usually 250 words or fewer), Additional Information section (context for anything unusual in the application). Analysis of strong examples in each type. Students identify which types their schools require and begin planning their approach.
student_work_product: Supplement plan by type and school

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Supplement Drafting — Session A
description: Working session: students draft 'Why Us?' essays for top 2-3 schools. Teacher circulates to check for specificity — if the essay could be sent to a different school without changes, it needs more work. Students who finish early begin drafting Why Major or Diversity essays.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What genuinely excites you about the programs on your list that isn't about prestige or rankings?'

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Supplement Drafting — Session B
description: Working session: students draft remaining supplement types. Peer share on particularly challenging prompts — collective problem-solving. Teacher available for one-on-one support on any supplement type.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Supplement Revision + Upload
description: Revision session for all supplements. Peer review on 'Why Us?' essays — is this school-specific? Could it be sent anywhere else? Students make final revisions and upload all supplements to Common App or school-specific portals.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: The Complete Application Review Checklist
description: Before submission, the full application must be reviewed systematically. Students work through a comprehensive checklist: every section complete, no fields blank, activities list finalized, personal statement uploaded, supplements attached, recommendations requested and tracked, testing decisions made, fee waiver applied if needed. Teacher reviews with each student.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Fee Waivers, Testing Decisions, and Final Logistics
description: Fee waivers: who qualifies and how to apply. Testing: final decisions about whether to submit scores. Application to community colleges and trade programs: different processes, still benefit from strong personal statements. Students with questions about specific schools' processes get individualized support.
student_work_product: Fee waiver applied; testing decisions finalized

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Application Workshop — EA/ED Submission
description: Structured work session and submission day for students with Early Action or Early Decision deadlines. Pre-submission final read. Teacher clearance protocol: every EA/ED applicant receives a teacher review before submitting. Collective acknowledgment of what it means to submit. For students without EA/ED deadlines: continued progress on RD applications.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Application Workshop — Regular Decision
description: Extended work session for Regular Decision applications. Students who have not yet submitted finalize and submit. Students who have submitted continue scholarship work. Teacher available for support and review.
student_work_product: RD applications in progress or submitted

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Application Workshop — Continued Work and Wrap-Up
description: Final application work session. All remaining students submit. Collective reflection: the applications are in. Brief class acknowledgment — what was hardest, what surprised you, what you're most proud of.

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: What Did This Take? — Fortitude Reflection
description: Fortitude reflection. Students identify the hardest moment of the application process — not to dwell, but to name it clearly and recognize what they did with it. This is evidence of fortitude: you kept going when it was hard. Peer conversation: share one moment where you almost gave up and what you did instead.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What was the hardest moment of this process for you? What did you do with it? What does that tell you about who you are?'

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: Collaboration Reflection — Who Showed Up For You?
description: Students reflect on the support system they activated this unit: who wrote recommendations, who helped with essays, who sat with you when you were frustrated. Gratitude practice: students write or share a specific thank-you to someone who helped. Collaboration named as the skill that made this possible.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'Who showed up for you during this process in a way that mattered? What do you want to say to them?'

unit_name: Unit 3: The Application  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Submitted Applications
title: End-of-Unit Alma Synthesis + Celebration
description: Full end-of-unit structure: Teacher-facilitated communal reflection (10 min) — what this moment means for first-gen students and their families → Peer conversation (10 min): 'What do you hope someone reading your application will feel about you?' → Alma synthesis (10-15 min) → Closing celebration (10 min).
alma_integration: Full end-of-unit Alma structure

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Why Scholarships Matter — and Why Most Students Leave Money on the Table
description: Unit launch. Scholarships are money that never has to be repaid. Most students don't apply because the search feels overwhelming or the essays feel like too much on top of applications. The reality: smaller, local, and community-based scholarships have far better odds than national competitions. First-gen students are specifically prioritized by many programs. This unit is a strategic investment of time with real financial return.

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Communication Returns — What Does Scholarship Writing Demand?
description: Explicit Communication skill return. Scholarship applications require making a compelling case for yourself in a short space to an audience you don't know. The skills developed in 11th grade Unit 2 are exactly what scholarship writing requires. Students revisit their Communication development and name how it applies here.

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: The Scholarship Landscape — Types, Sources, and Realistic Odds
description: Overview of the full scholarship ecosystem: federal scholarships, national competitions, institutional scholarships (some schools automatically consider all applicants for merit aid through the admissions process; others require a separate application — students must check each school's policy), community foundations, local organizations, identity-based awards, employer-linked scholarships, field-specific awards. Realistic odds: local and community scholarships often have 5-20 applicants; national competitions have tens of thousands. Students learn to build a balanced scholarship portfolio.

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: How to Find Scholarships — and Avoid Scams
description: Legitimate search tools: school counselors, Willow platform, community organizations, employer programs, professional associations. Red flags and scams: application fees, guaranteed awards, unsolicited offers. Students leave with 5-10 legitimate scholarship targets identified, with deadlines, eligibility, and essay requirements noted.

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Building a Scholarship Tracker
description: Organizational infrastructure for managing multiple applications. Students build a scholarship tracker: scholarship name, source, award amount, deadline, eligibility, essay prompts, materials needed, submission status. Collaboration in action: some students benefit from sharing their tracker format with family members who can help monitor deadlines.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What scholarships on your list feel most genuinely connected to who you are and what you care about?'

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Eligibility Deep Dive — Finding the Right Fit
description: Students research their top scholarship targets in depth. What do past winners say? What does this organization value? Students narrow to 6-8 high-priority targets and develop a preliminary plan: which essays can be adapted from existing writing, which require original work.

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: What Makes a Scholarship Essay Work?
description: Analysis of strong scholarship essays across different types. What makes scholarship essays different from college personal statements — and how are they similar? Committees want to give money to someone both deserving and likely to use it well. Students develop evaluative criteria: specificity, authentic voice, clear connection to the scholarship's mission, evidence of impact.

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Adapting vs. Writing From Scratch
description: Strategic decision-making about scholarship essays. Many prompts overlap with existing writing: personal statement themes, 'Why this field?' questions, community impact narratives. Students audit existing writing against their scholarship prompts. Adaptation requires genuine revision for the specific audience — it is not copying.

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Scholarship Essay Drafting — Session A
description: First major writing session. Students work on their highest-priority scholarship essay. Key message: scholarship essays that feel generic lose. The specificity of your story combined with a clear connection to what this organization cares about is what wins.

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Scholarship Essay Drafting — Session B
description: Continued drafting. Students working on adaptation essays focus on genuine tailoring. Students writing original essays focus on finding the specific story that connects to this scholarship's mission. Peer read: does this essay feel written for this scholarship, or could it be sent anywhere?

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Scholarship Essay Peer Review
description: Structured peer review. Review criteria: Is this specific to this scholarship's values? Does it feel authentic? Is the connection between writer and scholarship mission clear and evidence-based? Students give and receive written feedback.

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Revision Session A
description: Students revise based on peer feedback, focusing on specificity and connection to scholarship mission. Teacher conferences with students who need more support.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What are you trying to say in this scholarship essay that you haven't quite found the words for yet?'

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Completing the Full Application Package
description: Beyond the essay: reference letters for scholarships, transcripts, activity documentation. Students inventory what they need for each scholarship in their tracker and identify anything missing. Equity note: some scholarships require documentation that can be harder to obtain — strategies for navigating this.
student_work_product: Full application package checklist by scholarship

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Revision Session B + Final Polish
description: Final revision of all scholarship essays. Students who have submitted their highest-priority scholarship move to the next. Teacher supports students in making strategic decisions about which applications are most worth completing given time remaining.

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Scholarship Submission Session
description: Working submission session. Students submit applications with tracker documentation. Collective acknowledgment: every application submitted is a real action with real potential. Reminder: scholarship search continues through winter and spring as new deadlines open.

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Scholarship Strategy Going Forward
description: Not all scholarships are due in fall. Students update their tracker with spring deadlines and build a continued search plan for January–April. Some of the most valuable scholarships arrive after admission, when comparing financial aid packages. Students note which scholarships could affect their spring decision.
student_work_product: Updated scholarship tracker with spring deadlines

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: Communication Reflection — How Did I Grow?
description: Explicit Communication durable skill reflection. Scholarship writing is Communication at its most distilled: making a case for yourself in limited space. Students identify one moment in this unit where they communicated something about themselves more effectively than expected. How will this skill serve them in college and beyond?

unit_name: Unit 4: Scholarships  |  Durable Skill: Communication  |  Milestone(s): Scholarship Applications Submitted
title: End-of-Unit Alma Synthesis
description: Alma-assisted reflection (15 min) on the full first semester: applications submitted, FAFSA underway, scholarships in motion. Peer conversation: what are you most proud of from the last four months? Teacher names what students have built.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma reflection (15 min): 'What did you do this semester that you didn't know you were capable of? What does that tell you about who you are becoming?'

unit_name: Unit 5: Managing the Wait  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Waitlist Strategy Plan
title: The Weight of Waiting
description: Unit launch for second semester. The applications are in. Naming the emotional reality of the wait — hope, anxiety, uncertainty — without amplifying it. Fortitude reframe: waiting is not passive. It is an active practice of staying grounded, continuing to move forward on things you can control, and managing uncertainty with intention.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What are you feeling as you wait? What is in your control right now? What do you want to focus on while the decisions come in?'

unit_name: Unit 5: Managing the Wait  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Waitlist Strategy Plan
title: What to Expect and When
description: Demystifying the decision timeline. EA/ED decisions: December. Regular Decision: most arrive March 15–April 1. Rolling admissions: decisions can come any time. Community college and trade program decisions: often faster. Understanding what each type of decision means — acceptance, denial, waitlist, deferral — and what the appropriate response to each is. Students track decisions in Willow.

unit_name: Unit 5: Managing the Wait  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Waitlist Strategy Plan
title: Navigating Incoming Decisions as They Arrive
description: Protocol for EA/ED results and any early decisions. What to do when a letter comes: read carefully — what does each outcome require next? Waitlist protocol preview. Rejection: naming that rejection is nearly universal in this process and says nothing definitive about worth or future success. Celebrating acceptances — individually and collectively.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'How are you taking care of yourself during this period of uncertainty? What is one thing in your control that you can focus on?'

unit_name: Unit 5: Managing the Wait  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Waitlist Strategy Plan
title: Continuing Scholarship Work
description: The wait is the right time for scholarships. Students return to their scholarship trackers, identify open deadlines, and continue applying. Some of the highest-value scholarships — community foundation awards, professional association scholarships, employer-linked scholarships — have spring deadlines. Extended working session with teacher support.

unit_name: Unit 5: Managing the Wait  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Waitlist Strategy Plan
title: Managing Rejection — Processing and Moving Forward
description: Explicit lesson on rejection. It will happen. How to process without catastrophizing: naming the feeling, understanding what rejection does and does not mean, recognizing that multiple equally strong students compete for limited spots. Identity-affirming reframe: who you are is not determined by a committee's decision. Peer conversation with structured protocol — genuine acknowledgment and forward movement.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What are you feeling right now? What does this decision say about you — and what does it not say? What do you want to hold onto about yourself regardless of any outcome?'

unit_name: Unit 5: Managing the Wait  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Waitlist Strategy Plan
title: Understanding the Waitlist — Strategic Response
description: Waitlist protocol. What a waitlist actually means. What to do: send a letter of continued interest (specific, enthusiastic, updated with any new accomplishments), complete the waitlist enrollment form, ask your counselor to advocate. Odds: highly variable by school. Strategic reframe: treat the waitlist as a real option while continuing to commit to alternatives.

unit_name: Unit 5: Managing the Wait  |  Durable Skill: Fortitude  |  Milestone(s): Waitlist Strategy Plan
title: End-of-Unit Alma Synthesis
description: Alma-assisted reflection on the waiting period. What has this taught you about yourself? What does it mean to hold uncertainty without losing yourself? Teacher names Fortitude explicitly: students who have been able to stay grounded, keep moving, and process difficulty without shutting down have demonstrated real strength.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma reflection (15 min): 'What have you learned about yourself during this waiting period? What will you carry forward?'

unit_name: Unit 6: Understanding Your Financial Aid Offers  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Award Letter Comparison Chart
title: Understanding Financial Aid Award Letters — Part 1
description: What a financial aid award letter is and what each component means: grants and scholarships (free money, does not need to be repaid), work-study (must be earned through campus employment), loans (must be repaid with interest). The critical distinction: many award letters misleadingly include loans in the 'financial aid' total. Students learn to identify true grants vs. loans and calculate net price by subtracting only free money from cost of attendance.

unit_name: Unit 6: Understanding Your Financial Aid Offers  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Award Letter Comparison Chart
title: Understanding Financial Aid Award Letters + Appeals Process
description: Deeper dive into award letters: cost of attendance components (tuition, room and board, fees, transportation, personal expenses), how the SAI affects award amounts, renewable vs. one-year awards. Financial aid appeals: possible and often successful — most students don't know this. When to appeal: changed family circumstances, competing offers, undisclosed context. How to appeal: contact the financial aid office, explain specifically, provide documentation. Students draft an appeal letter template.
student_work_product: Financial aid appeal letter draft (if applicable)
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What surprised you when you saw your actual numbers? What questions do you still have?'

unit_name: Unit 6: Understanding Your Financial Aid Offers  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Award Letter Comparison Chart
title: Comparing Your Financial Aid Offers
description: When students have their actual letters: how to compare offers across schools when letters use different terminology and formats. Collaboration in action — this is the family conversation. Students build their Award Letter Comparison Chart using actual or projected offers, translating each letter into a common format for side-by-side comparison.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'When you look at these real numbers side by side, what surprises you? What feels clearest? How are the numbers interacting with what you care about most?'

unit_name: Unit 6: Understanding Your Financial Aid Offers  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Award Letter Comparison Chart
title: Maintaining Financial Aid
description: What students need to do to keep their aid from year to year: satisfactory academic progress (SAP) requirements, maintaining enrollment status, annual FAFSA renewal. Institutional scholarships: GPA requirements vary — students need to know the renewal conditions for every award they receive. Common ways students inadvertently lose aid and how to avoid them.

unit_name: Unit 6: Understanding Your Financial Aid Offers  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Award Letter Comparison Chart
title: Financing Your Future: Understanding Student Loans
description: What students and families need to know before signing anything. Subsidized vs. unsubsidized: the difference matters. Federal vs. private: federal loans have income-driven repayment, deferment, and forgiveness options; private often do not. Monthly payment reality: students run repayment calculations for their own likely loan scenarios. Borrowing strategically: the minimum needed, not the maximum offered.

unit_name: Unit 6: Understanding Your Financial Aid Offers  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Award Letter Comparison Chart
title: Financing Your Future: Hidden Costs and Budget Realities
description: The costs that aren't on the award letter: textbooks, course fees, transportation home, personal expenses, technology. Students build a realistic monthly budget for their freshman year using their school's actual cost of attendance breakdown. Key insight: most students significantly underestimate the true cost of attendance — and the gap between aid and reality.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'How is your financial picture interacting with your sense of fit and belonging? What matters most to you as you look at the real numbers?'

unit_name: Unit 6: Understanding Your Financial Aid Offers  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Award Letter Comparison Chart
title: Financing Your Future: Working While in College
description: Work-study: what it is, how to access it, what kinds of jobs are typical, how it interacts with academics. Part-time work off campus: benefits and risks. Research on work and academic performance: small amounts of work often correlate with better time management; too much work can hurt outcomes. Students think through what working in college might look like for them given their financial situation and career direction.

unit_name: Unit 6: Understanding Your Financial Aid Offers  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Award Letter Comparison Chart
title: Financing Your Future: Net Cost Reality Check
description: Synthesis lesson bringing together all financial data: net price, loan projections, hidden costs, work income potential. Students finalize their Award Letter Comparison Chart with complete real-cost calculations for each school. This becomes a key exhibit in their financial thinking going forward. Milestone complete.

unit_name: Unit 7: What's It Worth?  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Personal Financial Decision Framework
title: Career Deep Dive — What Will This Actually Pay?
description: Students return to their Career Vision from 11th grade with a new question: what does this actually pay, at what stage of career, in what region? Labor market data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Salary ranges by experience level, geographic variation, and sector variation (nonprofit vs. private, urban vs. rural). Key insight: labor market outcomes are probabilities, not guarantees — but they're still important data.

unit_name: Unit 7: What's It Worth?  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Personal Financial Decision Framework
title: Automation Risk and Labor Market Resilience
description: Which fields are growing, stable, or at higher risk of automation? Not to create fear but to inform decision-making. Durable skills connection: graduates with strong communication, critical thinking, and adaptability skills weather labor market shifts better. Students evaluate their career direction against these trends.

unit_name: Unit 7: What's It Worth?  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Personal Financial Decision Framework
title: Budget Reality — What Does It Actually Cost to Live?
description: Students build a realistic monthly budget for life after graduation: housing, food, transportation, healthcare, utilities, student loan payments, phone, personal expenses, savings. Using regional cost-of-living data for the area they're considering. Key insight: most students dramatically underestimate living costs. This is the most clarifying lesson of the unit.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What surprised you most about what it actually costs to live? How does that change how you're thinking about your decision?'

unit_name: Unit 7: What's It Worth?  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Personal Financial Decision Framework
title: ROI — Applying the Framework Personally
description: Students return to the ROI framework from 11th grade Unit 2, now with their own specific data: actual net price for each program, actual salary data for their career direction, their monthly budget. They calculate and compare program-specific ROI for their top options. This is not a formula that produces a single right answer — it's a framework that surfaces trade-offs.

unit_name: Unit 7: What's It Worth?  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Personal Financial Decision Framework
title: Debt-to-Income Analysis — What's Reasonable?
description: What level of student loan debt is reasonable relative to expected income? General guidance: monthly loan payments should ideally not exceed 10-15% of gross monthly income. Students run this calculation for their own scenarios. Discussion: what does it mean to take on significant debt for a program you love? These are real trade-offs with no objectively correct answer — but they need to be made explicitly.

unit_name: Unit 7: What's It Worth?  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Personal Financial Decision Framework
title: Personal Risk Assessment
description: Every postsecondary decision involves risk — and different students have different risk tolerances and different safety nets. Students complete a personal risk assessment: How important is loan minimization to your family's financial stability? How confident are you in your career direction? What is your backup plan if this path doesn't unfold as expected? This is not pessimism — it's preparation.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What are you willing to risk, and what aren't you? What does that tell you about what matters most to you right now?'

unit_name: Unit 7: What's It Worth?  |  Durable Skill: Collaboration  |  Milestone(s): Personal Financial Decision Framework

title: How to Commit — The Practical Steps
description: The mechanics of committing. Submitting the enrollment deposit: what it is, when it's due (most schools: May 1), what it does and doesn't guarantee. Housing applications: deadlines vary — check immediately upon deciding. Declining other schools: how to do it graciously and promptly. Email template for declining. FAFSA and financial aid next steps after committing. Orientation registration.

description: The emotional work of closing doors. When you commit to one school, you decline the others — and some of those were programs you cared about. This lesson acknowledges that complexity. Gratitude practice: students write brief notes of thanks to teachers and counselors who supported them. Peer celebration: sharing decisions with the class. Collective acknowledgment of what this community of seniors has accomplished.
alma_integration: ⭐ Alma micro-reflection (5 min): 'What does it feel like to close these doors? What do you want to honor about the paths you didn't take? What are you most looking forward to about the one you chose?'
